claim: Any construction that may affect navigable airspace must file FAA Form 7460-1 under 14 CFR Part 77 at least 45 days before construction; the FAA aeronautical study typically takes 60+ days and issues a determination such as Determination of Hazard or No Hazard.
source_title: Notification of Proposed Construction or Alteration on Airport Part 77
supporting_excerpt: All applicants proposing any construction or alterations... that may affect navigable airspace must file a Notice of Proposed Construction or Alteration (Form 7460-1)... notification must be submitted 45 days prior to construction... typical processing time... at least 60 days.
caveat: Determination timelines are typical, not guaranteed; complex cases (plume, EMI) take longer.

claim: Knowing/willful violation of the Part 77 notice requirement is subject to a civil penalty of $1,000 per day until notice is received.
source_title: Notification of Proposed Construction or Alteration on Airport Part 77
supporting_excerpt: Persons who knowingly and willingly violate the notice requirements of part 77 are subject to a civil penalty of $1,000 per day until the notice is received.
caveat: Applies to knowing/willful failure to notice; not automatic for good-faith omissions.

claim: The FAA studied exhaust-plume impacts on flight safety via its Airport Obstruction Standards Committee and publishes a Technical Guidance Assessment Tool for Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact.
source_title: Technical Guidance Assessment Tool - Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact
supporting_excerpt: FAA's Airport Obstruction Standards Committee (AOSC) was tasked to study the impact exhaust plumes may have on flight safety.
caveat: Full PDF returned HTTP 403 on fetch; existence/purpose confirmed via FAA-hosted URL and search summary, exact contents not directly quoted.

claim: Vertical plume velocity of 4.3 m/s is a widely used screening threshold requiring analysis, with 10.6 m/s a higher screening threshold; plume turbulence can extend more than 1,000 ft above the top of a stack or cooling tower.
source_title: FAA Finally Issues Guidance on Plume Hazards to Aircraft from Power Plants
supporting_excerpt: plume velocities in excess of 4.3 m/s is or will be a potential hazard... a more rigorous analysis... should be used if the 4.3 m/s and 10.6 m/s screening thresholds are exceeded... significant turbulent effects of an exhaust plume can extend to heights of over 1,000 feet above the height of the top of the stack or cooling tower.
caveat: 4.3/10.6 m/s are CASA-derived screening thresholds, NOT a codified FAA numeric limit. Do not present as 'the FAA limit.' FAA evaluates plumes case-by-case.

claim: AC 150/5200-33C recommends 5 statute miles separation between the airport air operations area and a hazardous wildlife attractant that could move wildlife into approach/departure airspace, and a 10,000-ft criterion for turbine-aircraft runway ends.
source_title: Advisory Circular 150/5200-33C, Hazardous Wildlife Attractants on or near Airports
supporting_excerpt: the FAA recommends a distance of 5 statute miles between the farthest edge of the airport's AOA and the hazardous wildlife attractant if the attractant could cause hazardous wildlife movement into or across the approach or departure airspace.
caveat: 5 mi is a recommendation for the approach/departure-airspace case; other separations (5,000 ft piston; 10,000 ft turbine) apply to different scenarios.

claim: AC 150/5200-33C directs that detention basins remain dry between rainfalls, and where water may stand, be built with paved/concrete bottoms or ditch/swale design to suppress nesting-habitat vegetation.
source_title: Advisory Circular 150/5200-33C, Hazardous Wildlife Attractants on or near Airports
supporting_excerpt: detention basins should remain totally dry between rainfalls, and where constant flow of water is anticipated or where any portion of the basin bottom may remain wet, the detention facility should include a concrete or paved pad and/or ditch/swale in the bottom to prevent vegetation.
caveat: A wet retention pond (vs dry detention) is the specific concern; AC language addresses design intent for detention.

claim: AC 150/5190-4B (Sept 16, 2022), 'Airport Land Use Compatibility Planning,' is the current land-use compatibility AC and exists to help airports comply with grant assurances on obstructions, wildlife/bird attractants, and protection of persons/property on the ground.
source_title: Advisory Circular 150/5190-4B, Airport Land Use Compatibility Planning
supporting_excerpt: AC 150/5190-4B is intended to help airports comply with their grant assurances concerning all compatible land use issues, including obstructions and hazard to airport navigation, airport noise, wildlife and bird hazard attractants, and protection of persons and property on the ground.
caveat: Confirms the author's citation is current/correct; supersedes AC 150/5190-4A (model zoning) and 2012 RPZ interim guidance.

claim: Airport Sponsor Assurances #19 (Operation & Maintenance), #20 (Hazard Removal & Mitigation), #21 (Compatible Land Use), #22 (Economic Nondiscrimination), and #29 (Airport Layout Plan) impose binding obligations, including keeping an FAA-approved ALP current and restricting nearby land use to activities compatible with normal operations.
source_title: Airport Sponsor Assurances (AIP) / Order 5190.6C Appendix A
supporting_excerpt: 20 Hazard Removal and Mitigation: assure terminal airspace is cleared and protected by removing existing hazards and preventing future hazards; 21 Compatible Land Use: restrict the use of land in the vicinity... to activities compatible with normal airport activities; 29: keep the ALP current at all times.
caveat: Wording here is paraphrased from FAA summaries; pull verbatim assurance text from the PDF/Order 5190.6C before quoting. Compliance-order appendix fetch returned 403.

claim: Data centers house dozens of backup generators, many rated 1-3 MW each, collectively capable of producing as much power as a conventional power plant.
source_title: Data Centers' Use of Diesel Generators for Backup Power Is Commonplace and Problematic
supporting_excerpt: Data centers house dozens of industrial generators, many capable of producing between 1 and 3 megawatts (MW) of power each. Together, these generators are capable of producing as much power as a conventional power plant.
caveat: Ranges vary by facility; supports that on-site generation (and thus thermal/exhaust plume) is inherent to the use.

claim: A Loudoun County substation fire forced nearby data centers onto diesel backup power, audible and with detectable fumes from a neighboring parking lot.
source_title: Data Centers' Use of Diesel Generators for Backup Power Is Commonplace and Problematic
supporting_excerpt: A fire at an electrical substation forced data centers in Loudoun County to rely on backup diesel generators... shoppers in a nearby Walmart parking lot hearing the noisy generators and reporting smelling diesel fumes.
caveat: Local precedent showing on-site generation is exercised in practice, not just standby.

claim: Cooling-tower plumes are saturated exhaust air that becomes visible when water vapor condenses and may present fogging or icing hazards to surroundings.
source_title: The Environmental Impact of Data Centers
supporting_excerpt: A plume is a stream of saturated exhaust air leaving the cooling tower... visible when water vapor it contains condenses in contact with cooler ambient air... a cooling tower plume may present fogging or icing hazards to its surroundings.
caveat: General engineering description; fogging/icing severity is site- and climate-dependent.

claim: MWAA's Board approved a 20-year Master Plan in July 2025 envisioning growth to ~90 million annual passengers, a fifth runway, and 24 additional gates, subject to FAA approval.
source_title: New master plan for Dulles Airport envisions growth to 90 million annual passengers
supporting_excerpt: New master plan for Dulles Airport envisions growth to 90 million annual passengers... addition of a fifth runway and 24 more gates.
caveat: Master plan requires FAA approval before implementation.

claim: The Dulles fifth runway has been in the airport's designs since 1958, was in the 1985 master plan, and both the fourth and fifth runways were FAA-approved in 2005; the fifth runway parallels 12-30 on the south side (~10,500 ft x 150 ft).
source_title: Fifth runway at Dulles draws attention as expansion plans take off
supporting_excerpt: The fifth runway has been in the airport's designs since 1958 and was included in the previously adopted 1985 master plan. The FAA approved both the fourth and fifth runways in 2005... approximately 10,500 feet long and 150 feet wide... parallel to existing runway 12-30 along the south side.
caveat: Fifth runway is on the 12-30 (E-W) side; the data-center parcel is on 1L/19R (N-S). Do NOT claim the parcel is the fifth-runway footprint. Supports airfield-reserve discipline generally.

claim: Loudoun County ended by-right data-center development in March 2025; new data centers now require special-exception legislative review with public hearings.
source_title: Loudoun County, Virginia, Eliminates By-Right Data Center Development
supporting_excerpt: On March 18, 2025, the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors approved amendments that eliminated by-right development of data centers, and now data centers are required to seek and obtain approval of a special exception.
caveat: County zoning process is separate from MWAA's airport ALP/7460 process, but signals heightened scrutiny even off-airport.

claim: Virginia regulators in Dec 2025 were weighing expanded use of data-center diesel backup generators, confirming on-site generation is standard practice in the IAD-area market.
source_title: Virginia regulators weigh expanded use of data centers' polluting generators
supporting_excerpt: Virginia regulators weigh expanded use of data centers' polluting generators.
caveat: Regulatory debate confirms prevalence of on-site generation; does not by itself establish airspace impact.
